newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-New jobs survey effect now undiscernible - ABS.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-New jobs survey effect now undiscernible - ABS.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Statistics said on Thursday the effect on jobs data of the implementation of telephone interviewing was no longer discernible.
The implementation of the new method, replacing a survey conducted entirely face-to-face, had only affected data earlier in the seven-month phase-in period, the bureau said.
"On the basis of latest data and analysis, this implementation effect has dissipated over the final months of implementation and is no longer discernible," it said.
"Therefore, the estimates for February 1997 and onwards are directly comparable to estimates for periods prior to August 1996."

A spokesman for the bureau said the seemingly transient implementation effect had built up until from August, when the new method began, until it had depressed the November employment estimate by 36,000 to 48,000.
The data since then was consistent with it having faded away to something statistically insignificant, he said.

However, the spokesman declined to reveal the original data from which the telephone effect is judged: the difference between employment estimates produced by the face-to-face and telephone methods during the phase-in months.
The data would be open to misinterpretation unless carefully explained, he said.
The bureau has previously said the new method's effect on employment was a cumulative minus 6,000 to minus 9,000 a month.
The new estimate of an accumulated effect in November of minus 36,000 to 48,000 implies a cumulative monthly effect of minus 10,500 in the first four months of the seven-month phase in period.
If the accumulated effect on February is zero, as the bureau says, then the cumulative implementation effect must have become plus 14,000 a month in December, January and February.
The bureau initially said the implementation of telephone interviewing would have "no noticeable" effect on the data.
Sources familiar with the data told Reuters in December that a quite noticeable effect had emerged, although the bureau responded by repeating its assurance.

But in the following release, the December data issued in mid January, the bureau said there was an effect, quantified it at minus 6,000 to minus 9,000 on employment but said the effect on other data, such as unemployment numbers, was indistinct.
The same message was repeated in the January data.
With Wednesday's data, for February, the bureau has all of the comparative information about the telephone effect it will ever have, because the phase-in is now complete.
